newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Televisa names Azcarraga as chairman.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Televisa names Azcarraga as chairman.

text.p: Emilio Azcarraga Jean, the son of the late chairman at Mexican media giant Grupo Televisa SA, on Wednesday officially took over his father's post after being named chairman of the board.

Azcarraga Jean, 29, replaced Guillermo Canedo White, a respected former CFO at Televisa, who was tapped as chairman by the late Emilio Azcarraga Milmo, the legendary leader at Televisa for 25 years until his death last week.
Canedo White, 37, was in turn named president of Televisa's Executive Committee, a newly-formed body that will play a key role in the company's operations and finances, company officials said.

The decision, approved by shareholders at an annual meeting in Mexico City, began to clear a controversy that had surrounded the company in the past few days amid reports that rival groups of shareholders were battling for power.

"It was logical that Azcarraga Jean be named as chairman. He is the single largest shareholder and was the only possible heir," Francisco Rivero, an analyst at Valores Finamex brokerage in New York, told Reuters.

But Azcarraga Jean's rise to the helm at Televisa came sooner than expected, especially after his father's recent decision to have his son share power at least temporarily until he was ready to take over the family empire.
And the move left lingering questions about the Spanish- speaking world's largest media firm.
"The only thing that makes me wonder was the timing. There must have been something going on to have forced the change so quickly after Azcarraga Milmo's death," Rivero said.

Investors, worried that the more experienced Canedo White had lost some influence at the company, did not appear to have reacted well to the news, driving down Televisa's stock price 1.70 pesos to 99 pesos on the Mexican stock market.

According to Mexican newspapers, problems were afoot at Televisa due to rivalry between Canedo White and either Azcarraga Jean or Alejandro Burillo, a former vice-chairman at Televisa who owns about 15 percent of the voting shares.

Televisa had kept silent on the reported split in its ranks, but a source close to the company told Reuters on Wednesday: "The result (of the shareholders' meeting) should kill all rumors of a split between groups of control in the company."

The source said several prominent international businessmen were named to the executive committee, including Claudio X. Gonzalez, head of Kimberly-Clark de Mexico, Luis Maria Anson, director general at Spanish newspaper ABC, and David Evans, a vice-president at News Corp .

Although analysts applauded the creation of the executive committee, which was seen as a move to help the company change from a family business to a professionally-run company, they wondered how much real power it would hold.
"How much Azcarraga Jean actually heeds the advice of the committee is an open question," said Marla Marron, an analyst at ING Barings in New York.
